Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 1 (SDG1) Despite significant reductions in poverty, rural and urban poverty persist in India. How can India balance economic growth with inclusive poverty eradication strategies under SDG 1.1 and 1.3? Strategies for Inclusive Growth Aligned with SDG 1.1 and 1.3 India has made commendable progress in poverty reduction. According to the World Bank’s Poverty and Equity Brief 2025, extreme poverty (measured at $2.15/day in PPP terms) declined from 16% in 2011–12 to 2.3% in 2022–23. Rural and urban poverty fell to 2.8% and 1.1%, respectively. However, ground-level disparities persist, particularly in vulnerable and historically marginalised regions, underscoring the need for a holistic and inclusive poverty eradication strategy. 1. Enhancing Livelihood Opportunities • Skill Development & Entrepreneurship: Expand programs such as Swavalamban, PMKVY, and NAP to build employability and promote self-reliance, particularly among youth and women in underserved areas. • Agriculture & Allied Sectors: Make agriculture more remunerative through diversification (e.g., dairy, poultry, food processing), better access to inputs, and improved market linkages. • Rural Infrastructure: Invest in roads, storage, and market infrastructure through schemes like PMGSY to reduce rural-urban economic gaps. • Non-Farm Rural Employment: Generate opportunities in sectors like food processing and services through targeted skilling (e.g., DDU-GKY) and credit access. 2. Targeted Social Protection (SDG 1.3) • Universal Insurance Coverage: Accelerate efforts to meet IRDAI’s goal of insurance for all by 2047, especially in rural areas. Ensure that health and medical insurance are affordable and accessible. • Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT): Strengthen DBT systems via Aadhaar-linked accounts for efficient and transparent subsidy delivery. • Employment and Pension Schemes: Enhance schemes like MGNREGS and NSAP to ensure income security and protection against life-cycle risks. • Universal Social Registry: Establish a dynamic, integrated database to identify and reach eligible beneficiaries effectively. 3. Inclusion of Marginalised and Vulnerable Groups • Create a supportive ecosystem for communities historically excluded from development, such as tribal populations in Jharkhand and the Northeastern states. • Tailor policies to address their specific socio-economic challenges and improve access to education, healthcare, and markets. 4. Urban Inclusion and Informal Sector Support • Expand affordable rental housing and urban skilling programs. • Leverage platforms like the E-Shram portal to improve informal workers' access to social security and entitlements. 5. Human Capital Development • Ensure universal access to quality education and healthcare as a long-term poverty reduction strategy. • Strengthen nutrition interventions like POSHAN Abhiyan and the Mid-Day Meal Scheme to address malnutrition and improve learning outcomes. • Promote awareness and behavioural change related to calorie intake and obesity through mechanisms like the Sugar Board. 6. Demographic Management and Labour Policy • Implement effective population control measures to convert the demographic dividend into a growth asset rather than a liability. • Develop a modern, inclusive labour policy to ensure fair wages, social security, and mobility, particularly in the gig and informal economy. 7. Fiscal Policy and Redistribution • Adopt progressive taxation to fund social investments without fiscal stress. • Redirect subsidies toward the most vulnerable through well-targeted schemes like PM Ujjwala (LPG) and the

Inclusive Strategies for Poverty Eradication in Line with SDG 1.1 and 1.3 Progress So Far According to the World Bank’s Poverty and Equity Brief 2025, India has made significant strides in poverty reduction: • Extreme poverty (defined at $2.15/day in PPP terms) fell from 16% in 2011–12 to 2.3% in 2022–23. • Rural and urban poverty declined to 2.8% and 1.1%, respectively. • Despite this, multidimensional poverty remains high. The 2024 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) by UNDP and Oxford reports India has the highest number of people living in multidimensional poverty, underscoring the need for inclusive development, not just economic growth. Strategic Focus Areas 1. SDG 1.1: Ending Poverty in All Its Forms a. Skill Development and Education • Expand access to skilling programs (PMKVY, DDU-GKY, Swavalamban) to improve employability. • Prioritize youth engagement to prevent diversion towards anti-social elements and ensure workforce readiness. • Promote vocational education with stipends and mandatory training modules. b. Rural Economic Strengthening • Improve agricultural productivity and promote allied sectors (dairy, poultry, food processing). • Expand rural infrastructure (roads, storage, markets) via schemes like PMGSY. • Encourage non-farm rural employment through entrepreneurship support. c. Urban Inclusion • Strengthen urban livelihoods via affordable rental housing, skilling initiatives, and informal sector protections. • Enhance platforms like the E-Shram portal for worker entitlement access. 2. SDG 1.3: Implementing Social Protection Systems a. Insurance and Pension Coverage • Accelerate IRDAI’s goal of “insurance for all by 2047.” • Expand health, life, and pension coverage under schemes like PMJAY, Atal Pension Yojana, and NSAP. • Ensure affordability and penetration in remote and rural areas. b. Digital and Technological Innovations • Leverage CBDC (Central Bank Digital Currency) with programmable features to ensure targeted subsidy transfers and minimize leakage. • Implement a Universal Social Registry for dynamic identification of eligible beneficiaries. c. Employment Guarantees and Direct Transfers • Strengthen MGNREGS to provide employment during lean agricultural periods. • Continue Direct Benefit Transfers (DBTs) using Aadhaar for transparency and efficiency. Cross-Cutting Measures for Sustainable Poverty Reduction 1. Fiscal and Taxation Reforms • Introduce progressive taxation, surcharges, and cess on top 1% income earners to address inequality. • Improve public spending efficiency and redirect subsidies toward vulnerable groups (NFSA, PM Ujjwala). 2. Human Capital Investment • Ensure universal access to quality healthcare and education. • Implement price controls for essential medicines via NPPA and monitor essential goods through the Essential Commodities Act. 3. Gender and Social Equity • Increase Female Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) through maternity benefits, childcare support, and menstrual leave. • Eliminate discrimination based on caste, gender, or ethnicity. As sociologist André Béteille emphasizes, social identity remains a major cause of poverty in India.

Regional and Sectoral Priorities • Focus on historically marginalized regions such as the tribal belts of Jharkhand and Northeast India. • Promote cooperative societies and empower local governments to boost rural enterprise and participation. • Protect vulnerable sectors like agriculture and dairy from cheap imports and encourage high-value exports (e.g., textiles, fisheries). Tackling Poverty in India: Strategies Aligned with SDG 1.1 and 1.3 Current Status India has made commendable progress in poverty reduction: • NITI Aayog’s National MPI 2024 reports a decline in multidimensional poverty from 25% (2015–16) to 11.28% (2019–21), lifting over 24.82 crore people out of poverty. • World Bank and ILO (2025) highlight a fall in extreme poverty from 27% to 5.3%, and an increase in social protection coverage from 22% to 64.3% between 2016 and 2025. Despite these gains, income inequality, urban-rural disparities, and persistent vulnerabilities highlight the need for a more integrated, adaptive, and accountable approach. Key Strategies for Achieving SDG 1.1 and 1.3 1. Employment Generation and Skill Development • Scale up schemes such as MGNREGA, DDU-GKY, PM Kaushal Vikas Yojana, and PM SVANidhi to provide employment opportunities, especially during lean periods. • Empower gig and informal sector workers through upskilling and formalization to ensure decent incomes and stable employment. • Leverage MSMEs, which contribute nearly 45% of exports, for job creation through targeted credit, policy support, and scheme integration (e.g., Mudra Yojana). 2. Social Protection and Financial Inclusion • Expand and deepen PMJDY, PM-KISAN, and National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) for financial security. • Increase pension and health insurance coverage under schemes like Ayushman Bharat and Atal Pension Yojana, especially to protect households from health-related impoverishment. • Encourage the use of programmable digital tools (e.g., CBDC) for targeted subsidies and to reduce leakages and corruption. 3. Affordable Housing and Basic Services • Strengthen access to housing, clean cooking fuel, and basic sanitation through PM Awas Yojana, Ujjwala Yojana, and Swachh Bharat Mission to improve quality of life and well-being. 4. Health and Nutrition Security • Ensure universal access to nutrition and healthcare services through programs like POSHAN Abhiyaan, PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, and Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana. • Prioritize preventive care and coverage in rural and low-income areas. 5. Women Empowerment and Rural Development • Promote Self-Help Groups (SHGs) under DAY-NRLM, expand access to credit and training, and support women's participation in the workforce through Stand-Up India and maternity-related provisions. Systemic and Structural Reforms 1. Strengthening Delivery and Implementation • Focus on outcome-based governance, not just scheme creation. • Integrate technology (AI, blockchain, GIS) for beneficiary tracking, transparency, and real-time monitoring. 2. Migration-Aware and Urban-Centric Policy • Design portable social protection frameworks for internal migrants. • Expand services like affordable urban housing, rental assistance, and informal worker registration. 3. Climate-Resilient Poverty Reduction • Recognize climate vulnerability as a poverty multiplier. • Integrate climate action with poverty reduction, especially in agriculture, housing, and disaster risk mitigation. 4. Behavioural Insights for Inclusion

Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 4 • Use nudges, such as targeted SMS reminders, to encourage enrolment in social schemes and improve public awareness. • Address cybersecurity risks to build trust in digital platforms. 5. Inclusive Data and Measurement • Move from household expenditure surveys to income-based assessments to better track inequality and target policies effectively. 6. Structural Reforms in Core Sectors • Strengthen healthcare, education, and skilling infrastructure with a focus on quality, access, and accountability. • Improve agricultural income by: o Enhancing crop productivity, o Reducing post-harvest losses, o Expanding cold storage and supply chains. (SDG 2- Zero hunger) What policies and programs have been introduced recently to address hunger and malnutrition in India, and are they inclusive and effective? Addressing Hunger and Malnutrition in India: Recent Programs and Policy Interventions India continues to face a dual burden of malnutrition—both undernutrition and micronutrient deficiencies, especially among vulnerable groups such as children, pregnant and lactating women, and adolescent girls. The government has launched a series of integrated initiatives targeting food security, maternal and child nutrition, agricultural resilience, and healthcare access. 1. Nutrition-Specific Interventions a. POSHAN Abhiyaan and Mission POSHAN 2.0 • A comprehensive mission focusing on improving nutritional outcomes for children, pregnant and lactating women, and adolescent girls. • Merged POSHAN Abhiyaan, ICDS, and Scheme for Adolescent Girls. • 2025 Budget Allocation: ₹21,960 crore; benefiting ~8 crore children, 1 crore pregnant women, and 20 lakh adolescent girls. • Saksham Anganwadi initiative supports infrastructure strengthening and capacity building. • Over 6.79 crore POSHAN Pakhwada activities conducted nationwide to promote awareness and community involvement. b. Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) • One of the oldest and most expansive schemes delivering supplementary nutrition, immunization, and health checkups through Anganwadi centers. c. PM Matru Vandana Yojana • Provides conditional cash incentives to pregnant and lactating women to promote health-seeking behaviour and nutrition. d. Food Fortification Initiatives • Rice Fortification under the PDS and mid-day meals to address widespread micronutrient deficiencies. • Expansion of fortified staples (iron, folic acid, Vitamin B12) across key food delivery programs. 2. Food Security and Hunger Alleviation a. PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY) • Launched in 2020 to address pandemic-induced hunger by providing free food grains to over 80 crore beneficiaries under the National Food Security Act. b. Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) • Targets the poorest of the poor, providing 35 kg of food grains per household per month at subsidized rates. c. One Nation, One Ration Card (ONORC) • Ensures portability of food entitlements across states, especially benefiting migrant workers and their families. d. Procurement and Price Stabilization

# Page 5^page=5
Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 5 • Government procurement of food grains ensures price support to farmers and a buffer stock for welfare schemes. • Export restrictions on essential crops are imposed as needed to stabilize domestic food prices. 3. Nutrition-Linked Health Interventions a. Eat Right India Movement • Promotes safe, healthy, and sustainable diets, with a focus on reducing consumption of high-fat, salt, and sugar foods. b. Jan Aushadhi Kendras • Provide affordable generic medicines to economically weaker sections, supporting better health outcomes and reduced out-of-pocket expenditures. 4. Agricultural and Allied Sector Support a. Crop Yield and Diversification • PM-AASHA, PMFBY, and Per Drop More Crop aim to improve yield, crop insurance access, and water- efficient farming. • National Millet Mission promotes nutri-cereals as part of a climate-resilient and nutrition-rich food system. b. Promotion of Allied Activities • Support for fisheries, poultry, and animal husbandry through dedicated schemes to enhance rural incomes and diversify nutritional sources. c. Local Food Systems • Encouragement of locally produced and seasonal foods through community awareness campaigns and POSHAN Tracker data integration. 5. Women-Centric and Community-Based Programs a. Mission Shakti • Integrates women’s safety, empowerment, and welfare, with indirect nutritional benefits through better health and financial security. b. Community Awareness & Behavioural Change • Behaviour change communication strategies embedded within schemes like POSHAN Pakhwada and Jan Andolan aim to transform household nutrition practices. India’s Initiatives Toward Achieving SDG-2 (Zero Hunger) India has made significant strides in addressing hunger and malnutrition through a range of targeted policy interventions and welfare programs. These initiatives focus on enhancing food and nutrition security, especially for vulnerable groups such as women, children, and economically disadvantaged populations. Key Initiatives and Programs 1. Saksham Anganwadi and Mission POSHAN 2.0 • An integrated nutrition support program targeting children, adolescent girls, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. • Aims to reduce stunting, wasting, and undernutrition, while promoting nutritional awareness through community engagement. • Consolidates various schemes under one umbrella, including Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) and POSHAN Abhiyaan. 2. PM POSHAN Abhiyan (Mid-Day Meal Scheme) • Provides hot cooked meals and take-home rations to school children to improve child nutrition, encourage school attendance, and support learning outcomes. 3. PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY) • Launched during the COVID-19 pandemic to provide free 5 kg of food grains per person per month to over 80 crore beneficiaries. • Played a vital role in alleviating hunger during economic disruptions caused by the pandemic. 4. National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013 • Ensures access to subsidized food grains for nearly two-thirds of the population through the Public

# Page 6^page=6
Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 6 Distribution System (PDS). • Special focus on priority households and Antyodaya beneficiaries (poorest of the poor). 5. One Nation, One Ration Card (ONORC) • Enables portability of food entitlements across states, ensuring food security for migrant workers and their families. 6. Rice and Food Fortification • Nationwide implementation of fortified rice distribution through PDS, mid-day meals, and ICDS to address micronutrient deficiencies, particularly in iron and folic acid. 7. National Health Mission (NHM) • Though primarily a health initiative, NHM plays a complementary role in addressing malnutrition through maternal and child health services, immunization, and health education. Impact and Challenges • According to NFHS-5 (2019–21), India has seen modest improvements in nutrition indicators: o Stunting in children declined from 38.4% (NFHS-4) to 35.5%. o Wasting and underweight prevalence have also marginally decreased. • These improvements reflect the positive effects of government schemes, especially those focused on maternal and child nutrition. However, the Global Hunger Index (2023) ranks India 105th out of 125 countries, highlighting persisting issues such as: • Child undernutrition, particularly in rural and tribal areas. • Micronutrient deficiencies due to poor dietary diversity. • Implementation bottlenecks and underutilization of allocated funds in certain states. Way Forward 1. Data-Driven Targeting: Utilize real-time monitoring tools like the POSHAN Tracker for improved beneficiary tracking and scheme delivery. 2. Community Participation: Strengthen local governance and community-led nutrition campaigns to ensure last-mile coverage and behavioural change. 3. Integration with Health and Agriculture: o Link nutrition efforts with maternal and child health services. o Promote nutri-cereal cultivation (e.g., under the Millet Mission) to diversify diets and improve food security. 4. Focus on Migrants and Urban Poor: o Expand urban nutrition initiatives. o Ensure portability and digital access to entitlements via ONORC. 5. Policy Synergy and Accountability: o Enhance inter-sectoral coordination between ministries. o Build accountability frameworks at the state and district levels for scheme implementation. (SDG 3- Good health and well being) How can India strengthen healthcare infrastructure to achieve universal health coverage while addressing NCDs and infectious diseases? Strengthening India’s Healthcare System: Key Strategies and Policy Recommendations India’s healthcare system has made significant strides in areas like digital health, insurance penetration, and infrastructure development. However, challenges remain in terms of accessibility, affordability, quality, and equitable delivery. To address these gaps, the following targeted measures are proposed: 1. Digital Transformation of Healthcare • Universal Digital Health Records: Implement a national digital health record for every citizen to enable better diagnosis, continuity of care, and efficient resource allocation under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. • Telemedicine Infrastructure: Expand video consultation facilities in government hospitals, especially in rural

# Page 7^page=7
Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 7 and underserved regions. Leverage platforms like eSanjeevani and strengthen digital connectivity at primary health centers. • Health Data Governance: Establish robust data privacy and interoperability frameworks to protect patient data while enabling seamless sharing among authorized health providers. 2. Primary Healthcare and Infrastructure Development • Revamp Primary Health Centres (PHCs): Focus on upgrading PHCs and Health & Wellness Centres (HWCs) with skilled personnel, better diagnostic facilities, and regular medicine supplies. • Promote Aarogya Mandirs: Encourage the development of community-based micro health centers in rural areas to ensure easy access to first-line healthcare services. • Improve WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene): Integrate WASH initiatives with health programs to prevent communicable diseases, especially in schools and slums. • Bed-to-Patient Ratio: Invest in increasing hospital beds, intensive care units, and emergency care facilities, particularly in tier-2 and rural areas. 3. Health Financing and Insurance Reforms • Universal Health Coverage: Ensure that health insurance coverage, such as under PM-JAY, is expanded to include all vulnerable groups. • Simplify Insurance Claims: Streamline and digitize the insurance claim process. Establish ombudsman frameworks to handle grievances related to claim rejections and unethical practices by health professionals. • Health Spending: Gradually raise public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP, as per the National Health Policy target, to improve infrastructure, human resources, and R&D. 4. Regulatory Oversight and Accountability • Enforce Quality Standards: Develop a national compliance framework mandating that all hospitals—public or private—meet minimum facility, hygiene, and service quality standards. • Licensing and Monitoring: Introduce periodic performance audits and link hospital licensing to adherence to prescribed benchmarks. 5. Nutrition and Preventive Healthcare • Food Safety Regulation: Empower agencies like FSSAI to conduct stricter surveillance of food quality across supply chains. Educate the public on healthy dietary practices to prevent non-communicable diseases. • Nutritional Literacy: Promote campaigns linking balanced nutrition to disease prevention, especially in schools, urban slums, and tribal belts. “If your food is wrong, medicine is of no use. If your food is right, medicine is of no need.” — This principle underlines the centrality of nutrition to preventive healthcare. 6. Health Education and Behavioural Change • School-Based Health Education: Introduce basic health, hygiene, and first aid education from early grades. Include mental health and nutrition awareness as part of the school curriculum. • Community Health Workers: Strengthen training for ASHAs, ANMs, and Anganwadi workers to promote preventive healthcare practices at the grassroots level. 7. Learning from Global Best Practices • Decentralized Healthcare Delivery: India can adopt aspects of the British NHS model, particularly its emphasis on universal access, doorstep delivery of medicines, and focus on preventive care. • Public-Private Collaboration: Leverage the capacity of private hospitals for innovation while ensuring equitable public health outcomes through regulation and partnerships.

Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 8 (SDG 4- Quality education) What educational reforms or schemes has the government implemented recently, and how are they influencing learning outcomes across different groups? Transforming Education in India: Key Government Initiatives and Their Impact India has launched several strategic initiatives to reform its education system, ensuring universal access, equity, foundational learning, and 21st-century skills for learners. These efforts are aligned with the Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG-4): “Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all.” 1. National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 • Reimagines the education system with a learner-centric approach, emphasizing experiential and skill-based learning. • Replaces the old 10+2 system with a 5+3+3+4 pedagogical structure, integrating early childhood care, foundational literacy, and vocational training. • Encourages multilingual instruction, flexible curricula, and integration of technology across all levels. 2. PM SHRI Schools (PM Schools for Rising India) • Model government schools being developed with a focus on smart classrooms, green infrastructure, and innovative teaching practices. • Aims to set benchmarks in quality education, based on the principles of NEP 2020. 3. Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan • A holistic scheme integrating elementary, secondary, and teacher education under one umbrella. • Focuses on infrastructure development, learning enhancement, gender equity, and inclusive education, particularly for marginalized groups. 4. NIPUN Bharat Mission • National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy. • Targets foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3 across all states by 2026-27. • Essential for reducing dropout rates and improving long-term learning outcomes. 5. Digital Education Initiatives a. PM e-Vidya • Launched during the COVID-19 pandemic to promote One Nation, One Digital Platform. • Integrates platforms like DIKSHA, SWAYAM, and radio/TV-based education for remote learners. b. DIKSHA Platform • Offers digital learning content mapped to school curricula in multiple languages. • Enables teachers and students to access e-content, assessments, and training modules. c. SWAYAM • A Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) platform providing free higher education courses, helping bridge the urban-rural learning gap. 6. Skill Development and Vocational Education a. Skill India Mission • Offers vocational training and skill certification for youth and school dropouts. • Enhances employability by focusing on industry-relevant skills. b. ULLAS (Udaan for Lifelong Learning and Advancement in Society) • Focuses on adult education, especially for individuals above the age of 14, promoting digital literacy, financial education, and citizen-centric knowledge. c. Atal Tinkering Labs (under Atal Innovation Mission) • Encourage innovation among school students in areas like robotics, AI, and machine learning. • Builds a STEM-focused ecosystem at the school level.

# Page 9^page=9

Equity and Inclusion Measures • Mid-Day Meal Scheme (now PM POSHAN): Improves nutritional outcomes and boosts school enrollment and retention, especially among disadvantaged children. • Special Training for Adolescent Girls: Targets dropouts and out-of-school girls with STEM education and vocational training, ensuring gender equity. • Scholarship Programs (e.g., SHREYAS): Provide financial assistance for higher education to SC/ST/OBC and economically weaker sections. 8. Pedagogical and Co-Curricular Reforms • No Bag Day: Encourages physical well-being, creativity, and experiential learning by integrating sports, arts, and life skills into the school schedule. • Vocational Integration: NEP 2020 emphasizes the inclusion of hands-on vocational education from Grade 6 onwards, linking education with livelihood. (SDG 5- Gender equality) What cultural and structural shifts are essential to ensure gender equality and eliminate violence against women in India? Towards Gender Equality: Required Cultural and Structural Shifts Achieving genuine gender equality goes beyond legal provisions it requires a cultural transformation coupled with institutional reforms. The following cultural and structural shifts are essential to eliminate discrimination and violence against women: I. Cultural Shifts: Challenging Norms and Changing Mindsets 1. Challenge Patriarchy and Gender Stereotypes o Deconstruct traditional roles that limit women’s autonomy. o Encourage shared responsibilities in households and caregiving. 2. Promote Consent and End Victim-Blaming o Shift from a culture of silence to one of consent and accountability. o Educate youth on respect, boundaries, and dignity through schools and media. 3. Normalize Women’s Autonomy o Promote decision-making power of women in families, careers, and communities. o Reject the narrative of motherhood as a societal obligation or penalty. 4. Representation in Media and Pop Culture o Encourage balanced and empowering portrayals of women in films, advertising, and digital platforms. o Celebrate female achievers across diverse fields, not just traditional roles. 5. Educational and Early Socialization Reforms o Integrate gender sensitivity and equality modules in school curricula. o Promote co-educational spaces that teach collaboration, not competition, between genders. II. Structural Shifts: Building Inclusive Systems and Institutions 1. Strengthen Legal and Administrative Frameworks o Ensure stricter enforcement of laws related to domestic violence, sexual harassment, and trafficking. o Simplify access to legal aid, especially in rural and underserved areas. 2. Access to Education and Economic Opportunities o Ensure universal enrollment and retention of the girl child at all levels. o Promote vocational training and skill-building to enhance employability. 3. Promote Women’s Political and Corporate Representation o Increase women’s participation in decision-making bodies at local and national levels. o Encourage representation in leadership roles across public and private sectors. 4. Support Systems for Survivors of Violence o Provide safe shelters, legal aid, mental health care, and financial rehabilitation for survivors. o Establish community-based support systems and crisis response teams. 5. Gender-Responsive Budgeting and Policy Design

# Page 10^page=10
Sustainable Development Goals Group Discussion Telegram: We Learn Here 10 o Implement gender budgeting to ensure that women’s needs are central to fiscal planning. o Evaluate and redesign existing schemes (e.g., PM POSHAN) to ensure resource control by women beneficiaries. 6. Use of Technology for Empowerment and Safety o Develop and promote tech-based safety tools, helplines, and geo-tagging for emergency response. o Leverage digital platforms for education, financial inclusion, and awareness campaigns. 7. Language and Perception Reforms o Move away from labels like “vulnerable” to emphasize agency and resilience. o Recognize and value all forms of women’s labor, including domestic and informal work. (SDG 6- Clean water and sanitation) What integrated water resource management strategies are needed to improve water access and sanitation in both urban and rural India? Strategies to Improve Water Access and Sanitation in India Access to clean water and proper sanitation is fundamental to public health, economic growth, and environmental sustainability. India, with its growing population and urbanisation pressures, requires a multi-dimensional and long- term strategy to ensure water security and universal sanitation. I. Sustainable Water Management Strategies 1. Greywater Utilisation and Recycling o Promote reuse of greywater (from sinks, showers, laundry) for landscaping, toilet flushing, and agriculture. o Integrate community-level treatment plants in urban and rural settings. 2. Sponge Cities Concept o Adopt the Sponge City model (as seen in China) around metropolitan areas to manage urban flooding, recharge groundwater, and enhance water retention. o Use permeable pavements, green roofs, and urban wetlands. 3. Water Body Interlinking and Irrigation Network Expansion o Interlink major rivers, lakes, and canals to ensure equitable water distribution. o Build efficient irrigation systems to reduce dependence on monsoons and overextraction of groundwater. 4. Household-Level Water Auditing o Install individual household water meters to promote accountability and reduce wastage in urban areas. o Implement tiered pricing to encourage conservation. 5. Crop Diversification and Water-Efficient Agriculture o Shift away from water-intensive crops (like paddy and sugarcane) in water-scarce regions. o Promote drip irrigation, rainwater harvesting, and millets cultivation under schemes like PMKSY and the International Year of Millets framework. II. Sanitation and Infrastructure Upgradation 6. Modern, Planned Drainage Systems o Upgrade and maintain underground drainage networks in both rural and urban areas. o Prevent open defecation and untreated waste discharge by strengthening monitoring under the Swachh Bharat Mission 2.0. 7. Enhanced Storage and Infrastructure o Increase investment in multi-purpose modern dams, reservoirs, and check dams to ensure year- round availability. o Promote desilting and restoration of local tanks and ponds. 8. Protection of Natural Resources o Enforce bans on illegal sand mining to prevent aquifer degradation and saltwater intrusion. o Launch afforestation drives for groundwater recharge and catchment area protection. III. Governance, Policy, and Public Engagement

Robust National-Level Water Policies o Strengthen and replicate successful models like the Namami Gange Mission, Atal Bhujal Yojana, and Jal Jeevan Mission (Har Ghar Jal). o Integrate water use planning into urban and rural development policies. 10. International Collaboration and Technology Transfer • Collaborate strategically with countries like Israel to adopt advanced technologies such as desalination, water recycling, and efficient irrigation systems. 11. Public Awareness and Behavioural Change • Conduct sustained IEC (Information, Education & Communication) campaigns on water conservation and hygiene. • Engage community leaders, school curriculums, and media to foster a water-wise culture. (SDG 7- Affordable and clean energy) Can India meet its rising energy demands while transitioning equitably to renewable energy sources? What recent measures has the Indian government taken to promote clean and affordable energy, and are they accessible to all? India’s Ambitious Green Energy Transition: Overview Targets and Vision • 300 GW Renewable Energy by 2030 (Currently ~241 GW installed capacity) • Expansion of Nuclear Power from 5 GW to 50 GW • Development of Energy Storage Systems to ensure grid stability and sustainable supply Key Achievements So Far 1. 50% Non-Fossil Fuel Capacity Achieved (5 years ahead of target) 2. Rapid Renewable Capacity Addition: Nearly 28 GW added recently, making India the 3rd largest renewable capacity increase globally after China and the USA. 3. Mega Renewable Energy Parks: o Bhadla Solar Park, Rajasthan (2.2 GW) – one of the world’s largest single-site solar farms o Khavda Green Energy Park, Gujarat (30 GW planned solar & wind) 4. Grid & Storage Infrastructure Improvements: Enhanced collaboration between government and industry for smart meters, net metering, and energy storage pilot projects. 5. Manufacturing Boost: ₹24,000 crore for solar module manufacturing and ₹15,600 crore for battery storage under PLI scheme. 6. National Green Hydrogen Mission: ₹19,744 crore allocated to develop 5 million tonnes green hydrogen capacity. 7. Government Schemes: PM KUSUM, PM Surya Ghar Yojana, Solar Parks, and smart grid technologies implementation. Major Challenges • Financing: A $300 million funding gap to promote clean energy projects remains a bottleneck. • Dependence on Coal: India remains one of the largest coal importers with coal-based generation still accounting for ~219 GW (largest share). • Grid Stability: Managing demand fluctuations and integrating intermittent renewables (solar & wind) poses technical challenges. • Energy Storage: Storage technologies are crucial but currently limited, affecting renewable energy utilization. • DISCOM Financial Health: Despite net metering benefits, losses to power distribution companies (DISCOMs) affect sustainability of green transition. • Upfront Costs: Renewable infrastructure requires high initial investment, making affordable financing and subsidies critical. Current Energy Demand and Supply Scenario

Formalizing India’s Informal Sector: Unlocking the Demographic Dividend India boasts the world’s largest demographic dividend with a labor force of about 470 million, of which nearly 400 million (90-95%) work in the informal sector. This sector comprises agricultural laborers, construction workers, domestic helpers, street vendors, gig workers, small shop owners, and employees of micro and small enterprises (MSEs). Despite its immense contribution to the economy—providing nearly 90% of urban employment and accounting for about half of India’s GDP—the informal sector faces critical challenges: Key Challenges of the Informal Sector 1. Lack of Job Security: Many workers have seasonal or irregular jobs (e.g., agricultural laborers, festival workers). 2. No Social Security: Absence of benefits like Provident Fund (PF), Employees’ State Insurance (ESI), health insurance, or pensions leaves their future uncertain. 3. Irregular and Low Income: Workers suffer from income instability and no income parity. 4. Limited Financial Access: Many informal workers remain outside formal banking and credit systems. 5. Low Awareness: Poor knowledge about government schemes and formalization benefits among informal workers. 6. Compliance Burden on Employers: Micro and small enterprises fear penalties and high costs linked with formal labor laws and social security contributions. Why Formalization is Crucial • Social Security & Benefits: Ensures workers get PF, ESI, health coverage (e.g., PM-JAY), maternity benefits (PMMVY), and pensions (e.g., APY). • Financial Inclusion: Access to banking (Jan Dhan Yojana), credit (MUDRA loans), and insurance. • Skill Enhancement: Formal skill training programs (PM Kaushal Vikas Yojana, PM Vishwakarma, ULLAS) improve employability and productivity. • Stability & Fair Wages: Formal jobs provide more stable incomes and regulated working conditions. Steps to Formalize the Informal Sector 1. Mandatory Digital Identification: Registration on platforms like the e-Shram portal to create a unified database of informal workers. 2. Expand Social Security Coverage: Broaden schemes like ESI, EPF, PM-JAY, PMMVY to cover informal workers systematically. 3. Financial Access and Support: o Promote Jan Dhan Yojana and Mudra loans for working capital without collateral. o Provide personal loans and credit tailored for gig and informal workers. o Establish financial cushions and loan restructuring options during economic downturns (recession, lockdowns). 4. Wildlife Conservation Initiatives India leads several global and national programs to protect its rich wildlife: • Big Cat Alliance: A coalition of 27 countries working together to conserve seven big cat species. • Project Elephant (Since 1992): Focuses on elephant conservation and habitat management. • Project Tiger: Has successfully doubled the tiger population since inception. • Project Snow Leopard: Conducted its first census last year; Ladakh became the first state to implement it. • Lion Conservation: Gir National Park has recorded the highest growth in lion population. • Cheetah Reintroduction Initiative: Bringing back cheetahs to India to restore ecological balance. • India’s First Wildlife Corridor: Established along the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway to facilitate safe animal movement. • Additional efforts: Hornbill conservation in Tamil Nadu, Tahr deer conservation in Jammu & Kashmir, systemic plant conservation in Madhya Pradesh. Monitoring and Enforcement • Wildlife Protection Act: Provides the legal framework for conservation, prevention of poaching, and promotion of wildlife welfare. • Collaborative Local Efforts: Partnerships between government and local tribal communities foster shared responsibility for ecosystem health. • Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC): Oversees policy formulation and effective implementation. • Technological Advances: o Madhya Pradesh became the first state to use digital mapping for real-time tracking of illegal tree cutting. o Use of drones and AI surveillance for monitoring forests and wildlife. • Regular Population Surveys: Ongoing monitoring of endangered species like Asiatic lions and leopards to guide conservation interventions. • Community Engagement: Initiatives such as Amrit Sarovars engage local stakeholders to protect biodiversity. • Independent Audits: Committees evaluate progress on major projects like the Namami Gange rejuvenation program. Other Notable Initiatives • Plant a Tree in the Name of Your Mother: Encourages community tree plantation. • Namami Gange and Project Yamuna: River rejuvenation projects with ecological and social benefits. • Artificial Coral Reef Development: To protect marine biodiversity.

Ensuring Transparent Governance, Accessible Justice & Reduced Corruption in India (SDG 16) Introduction: Transparent governance, accessible justice, and corruption reduction are fundamental pillars for the growth and sustainability of any society, especially a developing country like India. However, India faces multiple challenges that hinder these objectives, including bureaucratic red-tapism, political interference, outdated systems, and weak vigilance mechanisms. To address these, a combination of digital innovation, institutional reforms, and citizen participation is essential. Challenges: 1. Bureaucratic Red-Tapism: Delays and excessive procedural formalities stall governance and justice delivery. Many innovative ideas fail to scale due to administrative inertia. 2. Negative Attitude & Corruption Culture: A system plagued by corruption often punishes honest officials, while shortcuts are normalized by citizens and officials alike. 3. Weak Vigilance & Political Influence: Independent institutions suffer from political interference, resource shortages, and outdated monitoring tools, weakening anti-corruption efforts. 4. Colonial Legacy: Outdated bureaucratic and judicial procedures reduce efficiency and limit access to justice for common people. Policy Measures: 1. Digitalization for Transparency: o Expand initiatives like Digital India, Government e-Marketplace (GeM), and DigiLocker to digitize services, reduce human interface, and minimize corruption opportunities. o Implement real-time tracking tools for case management (e-Courts) and public grievance redressal systems (CPGRAMS). 2. Strengthening Independent Institutions: o Ensure autonomy for bodies like the Lokpal, CVC, CAG, and State Lokayuktas to investigate and prosecute corruption without political pressure. o Adopt bipartisan procedures for appointing key officials to safeguard independence. 3. Judicial Reforms: o Set up more fast-track courts and strengthen alternate dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms like lok adalats and tele-law to reduce pendency and improve access. o Digitize court records and hearings to expedite justice delivery and improve transparency. 4. Audit and Accountability: o Conduct regular independent audits of government departments and schemes to detect and deter corrupt practices. o Establish performance review mechanisms for public officials to ensure accountability. 5. Citizen Engagement and Transparency: o Promote tools like the Right to Information (RTI) Act and platforms such as MyGov for public participation and oversight. o Mandate public consultations on key policies and projects to increase transparency. 6. Police and Bureaucratic Reforms: o Implement the Model Police Act for modern, accountable policing with citizen oversight. o Introduce single-window clearance systems at local levels to simplify governance and reduce opportunities for graft. 7. (SDG 17- Partnership for the goals) What recent efforts has the government made to mobilize global cooperation, funding, or knowledge sharing for SDG acceleration. The Government of India (GoI) has actively pursued several initiatives to foster global cooperation, mobilize funding, and facilitate knowledge sharing for accelerating Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These efforts encompass multilateral alliances, bilateral agreements, innovative financing mechanisms, and strategic partnerships: 1. International Solar Alliance (ISA): A global coalition aimed at enhancing solar energy capacity by providing technical expertise and funding support. ISA targets raising $100 million to finance solar projects worldwide. 2. International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA): Established in 2023 and joined by over 30 countries, this alliance promotes global conservation of big cats through intergovernmental cooperation, pooling funding, and sharing expertise. 3. Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI): Launched by India in 2019, CDRI serves as a knowledge-sharing platform to promote the design and construction of disaster-resilient infrastructure globally. 4. Renewable Energy Investment Fund: A joint $600 million fund by India and Japan supporting projects in solar energy, green hydrogen, battery manufacturing, and critical mineral processing. 5. Green Bonds: The Government plans to raise ₹48,000 crore through green bonds in FY26 to finance sustainable development projects, with ₹10,000 crore already raised in H1 FY26. 6. SDG Localization and Monitoring Tools: o SDG Index India: Tracks progress on SDGs at the state level. o Localized SDG Index: Measures SDG progress at the Gram Panchayat level, integrating local development needs. 7. GOI-UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (2023-2027): A partnership between NITI Aayog and the UN in India to enhance SDG localization and promote South- South cooperation. 8. UN India SDG Country Fund: Launched in April 2025, led by the UN Resident Coordinator in India, with an initial $3 million seed fund from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation to support innovative SDG-related projects. 9. G20 2023 SDG Action Plan and Triangular Cooperation: During India’s G20 presidency, the group adopted an action plan to mobilize development financing and established a Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) repository to accelerate SDG implementation. 10. International Commitments and Multilateral Pledges: Over 50 countries endorsed the Seville Commitment to triple Multilateral Development Bank (MDB) lending, increase domestic revenue mobilization, introduce innovative taxation, and establish sustainable finance standards. 11. Regional and Global Partnerships: o BIMSTEC: Cooperation among Bay of Bengal nations to promote regional development and diplomatic ties. o QUAD: A strategic grouping including India, the US, Japan, and Australia focused on security and development collaboration. o BRICS: A coalition representing the Global South to advocate for equitable trade, prosperity, and growth. o Bilateral Free Trade Agreements: Agreements such as with EFTA and CETA (UK) to boost trade, reduce barriers, and attract foreign investments. 12. International Education Collaborations: Bilateral agreements with universities including Southampton, Liverpool, and the University of Chicago to establish world-class campuses in India and enhance educational standards. 13.
